title: the refusal is about the returned `Promise`, not about the `async` keyword: a `Promise`-returning binding marked `@throws {never}` is refused identically
notes: specification/compatibility.mdx, "Foreign Boundary": "Calling an unannotated foreign runtime value MUST add the checked `panic` case, because JavaScript and TypeScript may throw, reject, or violate a declaration." `async` is sugar for returning a `Promise`, so a rule that keyed on the keyword would leave the sugar-free spelling fail-open — and this is the shape the next platform binding actually takes (a trusted `readFile` or `fetch` declared in a `.d.ts` returns `Promise<T>` and is not written `async`). The pair of cases is the evidence that the rule asks about the rejection channel rather than about a syntax.
